## Suit for Partition and Temporary Injunction

A SUIT FOR PARTITION, DECLARATION, SEPARATE POSSESSION, AND PERMANENT & TEMPORARY INJUNCTION

The suit is filed under the provisions of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, particularly Section 8 thereof, for partition and separate possession of the Plaintiff's share; under the Specific Relief Act, 1963 for a declaration of the Plaintiff's rights; and under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, for a temporary injunction restraining the Defendant from alienating or creating third-party interests in the suit properties.

## Facts of the Case

1. That the Plaintiff, Rupa, is the adopted daughter of Late [Father's Name] and the Defendant, [Mother's Name]. The Plaintiff has no siblings. The Plaintiff and the Defendant constitute a Hindu joint family.

2. That the Plaintiff's father, the late [Father's Name], passed away intestate approximately five years ago, leaving behind the Plaintiff and the Defendant as his only legal heirs and successors.

3. That during his lifetime, the Plaintiff's father had acquired two residential flats situated in Pune from his own earnings and savings. The said properties, hereinafter referred to as the "suit properties", are more particularly described in the Schedule of Properties annexed hereto.

4. That upon the demise of the Plaintiff's father, the Plaintiff and the Defendant, being his sole Class I heirs under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, jointly succeeded to the entirety of his estate, including the two suit properties. Consequently, the Plaintiff and the Defendant each have an equal, undivided one-half (1/2) share in the suit properties and are in joint possession thereof.

5. That despite the Plaintiff being a rightful co-owner, her name has not yet been mutated or entered into the official property records or documents pertaining to the suit properties.

6. That recently, the Defendant's behaviour towards the Plaintiff has become hostile. The Defendant has been attempting to dispossess the Plaintiff from the family home and has explicitly threatened to sell and transfer the suit properties to her cousin, thereby depriving the Plaintiff of her legitimate and legal share.

7. However, the Defendant has outright refused to do so and is actively taking steps to alienate the properties.

8. That the cause of action for the present suit first arose when the Defendant threatened to dispossess the Plaintiff and alienate the suit properties, and continues to subsist.

## Legal Provisions

9. That the parties are Hindus and are governed by the Mitakshara School of Hindu Law. The succession to the properties of the Plaintiff's deceased father is governed by the provisions of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.

10. That as per Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the property of a Hindu male dying intestate devolves upon the heirs specified in Class I of the Schedule to the said Act. The Plaintiff, being the daughter, and the Defendant, being the widow, are the only Class I heirs of the deceased and are therefore entitled to an equal share in his estate.

11. That the Plaintiff has a prima facie case and the balance of convenience lies in her favour. If the Defendant is not
restrained by an order of temporary injunction from alienating, transferring, or creating any third-party rights in the
suit properties during the pendency of this suit, the Plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss and injury which cannot be
compensated in terms of money. The very purpose of the suit would be defeated, leading to a multiplicity of proceedings.
This warrants the grant of interim relief under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

12. That the suit properties are situated within the territorial jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court.

13. That the suit is valued for the purposes of court fees and jurisdiction as per the Maharashtra Court Fees Act, 1959, and the requisite court fee has been paid thereon.

14. That the suit is filed within the period of limitation as prescribed under the Limitation Act, 1963.

## Plaintiff's Entitlement and Share

15. That the Plaintiff, being the legally adopted daughter of the deceased, holds the same status and rights as a
natural-born daughter under Hindu law. By virtue of Section 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, an
adopted child is deemed to be the child of his or her adoptive father or mother for all purposes with effect from the
date of the adoption. All ties of the child in the family of his or her birth are severed and replaced by those created
by the adoption in the adoptive family.

16. That upon the intestate demise of the Plaintiff's father, his entire estate devolved upon his Class I heirs as specified in the Schedule to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The Plaintiff (daughter) and the Defendant (widow) are the only two Class I heirs.

17. That accordingly, the Plaintiff is legally entitled to an equal, undivided one-half (1/2) share, right, title, and interest in all the assets left behind by her deceased father, including the two suit properties more particularly described in the Schedule hereto. The Defendant is entitled to the remaining one-half (1/2) share.

18. That the non-mutation of the Plaintiff's name in the property records does not, in any manner, extinguish or diminish her vested legal right in the suit properties. It is a settled principle of law that mutation of entries in revenue or municipal records is for fiscal purposes only and does not create or extinguish title to the property. The Plaintiff's title is derived by succession under the law, which is automatic upon the death of the intestate owner.

## Grounds for Temporary Injunction

19. That the Plaintiff has a strong prima facie case in her favour, as her status as a Class I heir and her entitlement to a 1/2 share in the suit properties is established by the provisions of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The Defendant has no right to deal with the entire property to the exclusion of the Plaintiff.

20. That the balance of convenience lies overwhelmingly in favour of the Plaintiff and against the Defendant. Granting
an injunction would only require the Defendant to maintain the status quo of the properties until the rights of the
parties are adjudicated by this Hon'ble Court, causing no prejudice to the Defendant's own 1/2 share. Conversely,
refusing the injunction would allow the Defendant to act upon her threats to alienate the properties, which would create
irreversible third-party rights, lead to a multiplicity of proceedings, and render the present suit for partition
infructuous.

21. That the Plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss and injury if the temporary injunction is not granted. The Defendant has explicitly threatened to sell and transfer the suit properties to her cousin to defeat the Plaintiff's legitimate claim. If such a transfer is effected, the Plaintiff will be wrongfully deprived of her rightful share in her family properties. The loss of an immovable property, especially a residential home, cannot be adequately compensated in monetary terms.

22. That the Defendant's actions are malafide and specifically intended to oust the Plaintiff from her legal inheritance. Therefore, it is just and necessary, in the interest of justice, that the Defendant, her agents, servants, or anyone claiming through her, be restrained by an order of temporary injunction from selling, transferring, alienating, mortgaging, or creating any third-party interest or charge in respect of the suit properties during the pendency of this suit.

## Jurisdiction and Valuation

23. That the suit properties are situated in Pune, which is within the territorial jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court. Therefore, this Hon'ble Court has the jurisdiction to try and entertain the present suit.

24. That the suit is for partition and separate possession of the Plaintiff's share in the suit properties. As the Plaintiff is in joint possession of the suit properties, the suit is valued for the purpose of court fees under Section 6(1)(vii) of the Maharashtra Court Fees Act, 1959, and the requisite fixed court fee has been paid thereon. A separate fixed court fee has also been paid for the relief of injunction.

(a) Pass a preliminary decree for partition, declaring that the Plaintiff is the owner of and is entitled to a one-half (1/2) undivided share, right, title, and interest in the suit properties more particularly described in the Schedule of Properties annexed hereto.

(b) Appoint a Court Commissioner to effect the partition of the suit properties by metes and bounds and, upon receiving the Commissioner's report, pass a final decree putting the Plaintiff in separate, vacant, and peaceful possession of her one-half (1/2) share in the suit properties.

(c) Pass an order of temporary injunction under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, restraining the Defendant, her agents, servants, assigns, or any person claiming through or under her, from selling, alienating, transferring, mortgaging, gifting, leasing, or creating any third-party rights, title, or interest of any nature whatsoever in the suit properties during the pendency of the present suit.

(d) Pass a decree of permanent injunction restraining the Defendant and her representatives from obstructing or interfering with the Plaintiff's possession and enjoyment of the suit properties.

(e) Award the costs of this suit to the Plaintiff from the Defendant.

(f) Grant any other and further relief as this Hon'ble Court may deem fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case and in the interest of justice.

### SCENARIO CITATIONS:
### Arguments for the Plaintiff (Mrs. Anjali Deshmukh)

The plaintiff, Mrs. Anjali Deshmukh, would argue that Dr. Rakesh Nair and XYZ Multispecialty Hospital are liable for medical negligence based on the following grounds:

1.  **Duty of Care:** Dr. Rakesh Nair, as the operating surgeon, owed a duty of care to Mrs. Anjali Deshmukh to exercise reasonable skill and care during the gallbladder surgery. Similarly, XYZ Multispecialty Hospital owed a duty to provide adequate facilities and ensure that its medical professionals adhered to the accepted standards of care. This duty arises from the doctor-patient relationship and the hospital-patient relationship.
2.  **Breach of Duty (Negligence):**
-   **Failure to Exercise Reasonable Skill and Care:** The core of the plaintiff's argument is that Dr. Nair negligently
damaged her bile duct during the surgery. This constitutes a breach of the duty to exercise the ordinary degree of skill
and care that a reasonably competent medical practitioner would have exercised in the same circumstances. The Supreme
Court has consistently held that a medical professional is expected to exercise a reasonable degree of care and skill,
and not every slip or error can be termed as negligence. However, a clear deviation from accepted surgical practice
leading to an injury that would not ordinarily occur without negligence can establish a breach.
    -   **Application of *Res Ipsa Loquitur*:** The principle of *res ipsa loquitur* (the thing speaks for itself) may be invoked, suggesting that the damage to the bile duct during a routine gallbladder surgery is an event that would not typically occur in the absence of negligence. While not a rule of law, it is a rule of evidence that shifts the burden of explanation to the defendant.
    -   **Violation of Accepted Medical Standards:** The injury to the bile duct indicates that the surgical procedure was not performed in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical men skilled in that particular art, as per the modified Bolam test applied in India.
3.  **Causation:** The negligent act of damaging the bile duct directly led to severe post-surgery complications, necessitating corrective surgery at another hospital. This establishes a direct causal link between Dr. Nair's negligence and the subsequent harm suffered by Mrs. Deshmukh, including additional medical expenses, physical pain, and mental agony.
4.  **Damages:** Mrs. Deshmukh is entitled to compensation for the damages incurred, including:
    -   **Medical Expenses:** ₹3.5 lakhs already spent on corrective surgery and related treatment.
    -   **Pain and Suffering:** Compensation for the severe pain and discomfort experienced due to the complications and subsequent surgery.
    -   **Mental Agony and Harassment:** Damages for the mental distress, anxiety, and harassment caused by the negligence, the need for further surgery, and the refusal of compensation.
    -   **Future Treatment:** Potential costs for any future medical treatment or follow-up care necessitated by the bile duct injury.

### Arguments for the Defendant (Dr. Rakesh Nair and XYZ Multispecialty Hospital)

The defendants, Dr. Rakesh Nair and XYZ Multispecialty Hospital, would contend that there was no medical negligence and would raise the following arguments:

1.  **Adherence to Standard of Care:** Dr. Rakesh Nair exercised the requisite degree of care and skill expected of a reasonably competent surgeon. The Supreme Court has clarified that a medical professional cannot be held liable for negligence merely because a procedure was unsuccessful or a complication arose, provided they acted with reasonable competence and followed accepted medical practices.
2.  **Inherent Risks of Surgery:** Gallbladder surgery, like any surgical procedure, carries inherent risks and potential complications, including bile duct injury, even when performed with due care and skill. Such complications can arise due to anatomical variations, unforeseen circumstances, or the complexity of the patient's condition, and do not necessarily indicate negligence.
3.  **No *Res Ipsa Loquitur*:** The defendants would argue that the principle of *res ipsa loquitur* is not strictly applicable in all cases of surgical complications. They would assert that bile duct injuries can occur despite the surgeon exercising all reasonable precautions, and thus, the mere occurrence of the injury does not automatically imply negligence. The burden remains on the plaintiff to prove specific acts of negligence.
4.  **Absence of Gross Negligence:** For a medical professional to be held liable in criminal negligence, the negligence must be of a "gross" or "reckless" degree. While this case is likely a civil claim, the standard for civil negligence also requires a clear departure from the ordinary standard of care, not merely an error of judgment.
5.  **Contestation of Quantum of Damages:** The defendants would challenge the quantum of damages sought by the plaintiff, arguing that the amount of ₹25 lakhs is excessive and not fully substantiated. They may argue that some components of the claim, such as mental harassment or future treatment, are speculative or not directly attributable to any alleged negligence. They would demand strict proof of all claimed expenses and losses.

### Relevant Case Laws

1.  *Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab, (2005) 6 SCC 1*
    -   **Court:** Supreme Court of India
    -   **Year:** 2005
    -   **Bench:** 3-Judge Bench
-   **Key Legal Principle / Ratio Decidendi:** This landmark judgment established the standard for medical negligence in
India, holding that a medical professional is not liable for negligence if he has acted in accordance with a practice
accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical men skilled in that particular art. An error of judgment is not
necessarily negligence. The negligence must be gross for criminal liability, while for civil liability, it must be a
failure to exercise reasonable skill and care.
2.  *Kusum Sharma v. Batra Hospital and Medical Research Centre, (2010) 3 SCC 480*
    -   **Court:** Supreme Court of India
    -   **Year:** 2010
    -   **Bench:** 2-Judge Bench
    -   **Key Legal Principle / Ratio Decidendi:** Reaffirmed the principles laid down in *Jacob Mathew*, emphasizing that doctors are not liable for every mishap or complication. It reiterated that a doctor must bring to his task a reasonable degree of skill and knowledge and must exercise a reasonable degree of care. A mere error of judgment or an accident, even if fatal, is not necessarily negligence.
3.  *V. Kishan Rao v. Nikhil Super Speciality Hospital, (2010) 5 SCC 513*
    -   **Court:** Supreme Court of India
    -   **Year:** 2010
    -   **Bench:** 2-Judge Bench
    -   **Key Legal Principle / Ratio Decidendi:** Held that in cases of medical negligence, the principle of *res ipsa loquitur* can be applied, particularly when the injury sustained by the patient is such that it would not have ordinarily occurred without negligence. The burden then shifts to the hospital/doctor to explain the circumstances.
4.  *Dr. Balram Prasad v. Dr. Kunal Saha, (2014) 1 SCC 384*
    -   **Court:** Supreme Court of India
    -   **Year:** 2014
    -   **Bench:** 2-Judge Bench
    -   **Key Legal Principle / Ratio Decidendi:** This case dealt with the quantum of compensation in medical negligence cases, affirming that compensation should be just and adequate, taking into account medical expenses, pain and suffering, loss of earning, and future prospects. It highlighted the importance of a holistic approach to assessing damages.
5.  *Malay Kumar Ganguly v. Sukumar Mukherjee, (2009) 9 SCC 221*
    -   **Court:** Supreme Court of India
    -   **Year:** 2009
    -   **Bench:** 2-Judge Bench
    -   **Key Legal Principle / Ratio Decidendi:** Emphasized the vicarious liability of hospitals for the negligence of their doctors, especially when the doctors are on the panel or employed by the hospital. It also delved into the assessment of damages for medical negligence, including for pain, suffering, and loss of enjoyment of life.

10. As per Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the property of a Hindu male dying intestate devolves upon the heirs specified in Class I of the Schedule to the said Act. वादी, कन्या असल्याने, आणि प्रतिवादी, विधवा असल्याने, मृत व्यक्तीचे एकमेव Class I heirs आहेत आणि म्हणूनच त्यांना त्याच्या मालमत्तेत समान हिस्सा मिळण्याचा हक्क आहे.

दावा मालमत्तांचे हस्तांतरण, विक्री किंवा त्यामध्ये कोणत्याही तृतीय-पक्षाचे हक्क निर्माण करण्यापासून तात्पुरत्या मनाई
हुकुमाद्वारे रोखले नाही, तर वादीचे भरून न येणारे नुकसान आणि इजा होईल, ज्याची पैशांच्या स्वरूपात भरपाई होऊ शकत नाही.
दाव्याचा मूळ उद्देशच निष्फळ होईल, ज्यामुळे अनेक कार्यवाही होतील. यामुळे Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 च्या Order XXXIX
Rules 1 and 2 अंतर्गत अंतरिम दिलासा मंजूर करणे आवश्यक आहे.

12. दावा मालमत्ता या माननीय न्यायालयाच्या प्रादेशिक अधिकारक्षेत्रात स्थित आहेत.

13. Maharashtra Court Fees Act, 1959 नुसार न्यायालयीन शुल्क आणि अधिकारक्षेत्रासाठी दाव्याचे मूल्यांकन करण्यात आले आहे आणि आवश्यक न्यायालयीन शुल्क भरले आहे.

14. Limitation Act, 1963 अंतर्गत विहित केलेल्या मुदतीत हा दावा दाखल करण्यात आला आहे.

## वादीचा हक्क आणि हिस्सा

15. वादी, मृत व्यक्तीची कायदेशीररित्या दत्तक घेतलेली मुलगी असल्याने, हिंदू कायद्यानुसार नैसर्गिक मुलीप्रमाणे समान दर्जा आणि हक्क धारण करते. As per Section 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, दत्तक घेतल्याच्या तारखेपासून दत्तक मूल सर्व उद्देशांसाठी त्याच्या दत्तक वडील किंवा आईचे मूल मानले जाते. मुलाचे जन्म कुटुंबातील सर्व संबंध तोडले जातात आणि दत्तक कुटुंबामध्ये दत्तक घेतल्याने निर्माण झालेल्या संबंधांनी त्यांची जागा घेतली जाते.

16. वादीच्या वडिलांच्या मृत्युपत्र न करता झालेल्या निधनानंतर, त्यांची संपूर्ण मालमत्ता devolved upon his Class I heirs as specified in the Schedule to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. वादी (कन्या) आणि प्रतिवादी (विधवा) हे एकमेव दोन Class I heirs आहेत.

17. त्यानुसार, वादीला तिच्या मृत वडिलांनी मागे ठेवलेल्या सर्व मालमत्तांमध्ये, ज्यात यासोबत जोडलेल्या परिशिष्टात अधिक तपशीलवार वर्णन केलेल्या दोन दावा मालमत्तांचा समावेश आहे, समान, अविभक्त एक-द्वितीयांश (1/2) हिस्सा, हक्क, मालकी आणि हितसंबंध मिळण्याचा कायदेशीर हक्क आहे. प्रतिवादीला उर्वरित एक-द्वितीयांश (1/2) हिस्सा मिळण्याचा हक्क आहे.
